seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: For the Record
blurb: Ada has sixteen warm pieces of a lantern nobody remembers owning, a Registrar who answers everything "for the record", and a ledger with one line left blank.

blocks.text: Ada's fingers were in the ashes.
The glass was warm. Not ember-warm. Warm like a cup someone has only just put down.
Over it the readout flickered, gold, then nothing, then gold, like a meter on a circuit that isn't there any more. Trying to measure something already broken.
Behind her, a floorboard creaked.
"Don't touch that," said a voice, precise as a ruler. "For the record, touching that is an offence."

He stood inside Odile's door, rain on his shoulders, a large book held to his chest like a shield. Young, thin, buttoned to the throat. He took his spectacles off to look at her, as if they were the problem.
"Emrys Vale. Registrar of Lanterns. I'm here to log an irregularity."
"What irregularity?" Ada asked.
"You."
From the back room, the clatter of a kettle and Odile's voice. "Is that Emrys? Did you knock? He never knocks. He just appears, like weather."

"I knocked," Emrys said. "Twice. Quietly." He turned back to Ada. "An outsider, practising as Mender, with no lantern and no line in the Register. And I find you with your hands in a grate full of—" He stopped, and put the spectacles back on. "Of lantern glass."
"I didn't break it."
"I didn't say you broke it. I said touching it was an offence."
"Is it?"
He considered. "It's an offence in the sense that I'm offended."
Ada nearly laughed. She didn't, because he had gone a shade paler looking at the glass.
Odile came through with three cups on a tray and a pin between her teeth. "What glass?"
Ada held up a piece. Odile looked at it, then at the hearth shelf, at the clean square in the dust.
"That spot's always been empty," she said. "Always. A bit of damp, or a cat sat there—"
"You haven't got a cat," said Emrys.
"Then a cat's been in." She set the tray down hard. "There's never been anything on that shelf. I'd know."
Emrys opened his book on the table: ruled brown lines, a name and a street on each in careful ink. He found Cutter's Row and ran a finger down.
"Fane's Alterations. One lantern registered to the house. Fane, Odile." His finger stopped. "One."
Ada leaned in. Odile's line. And under it, before the next house, one ruled line with nothing written on it.
Emrys shut the book, faster than he needed to. It was very loud in the little room.
"One lantern," he said. "For the record. It has always been one."
He lent her his handkerchief for the shards. "It's never been used," he said, when she hesitated. "I keep it for emergencies. This is the first."
Ada counted the pieces onto the white cotton. Fourteen, each the size of a fingernail, each faintly warm.
"That's not a lantern," she said. "That's a handful. A lantern's three times this."

"So where's the rest?" said Odile, and answered herself before anyone else could. "The bin. No. The— oh." She took the pin out of her mouth. "Everyone on the Row tips their sweepings off the end of the towpath. Below the bridge. Into the canal."
"Then someone cleaned up," Ada said, "and missed a bit. And tipped the rest."
Emrys wrote that down. Then he looked at the shelf and said nothing for so long that Odile offered him a biscuit.
Next morning the ferry was right there.
Old Nobody's flat black boat bumped against the Pell Street steps, water slapping under it. The ferryman lifted a hand.
"Name, miss?"
"Ada."
"Ada." He smiled. "Ada. Across?"
"Two of us," Ada said. "Cutter's Row, the towpath under the bridge. It's quickest."
Behind her, Emrys did not move.
He stood at the top of the steps, boots planted on the last dry stone.
"I don't take the ferry."
"It's two minutes."
"It's a rule of my office."
"Which rule?"
"Shall we walk round by the bridge? There's a woman on it who sells very good hot apples. And the weather's turning. Look at that sky." He was already walking.
Ada looked at the ferryman. The ferryman looked at her, kindly, and asked her name again.
The long way round was long: along the upper wall where gulls quarrelled on the railings, and over the bridge, its iron rail cold under her hand.
"You walk this every day?" Ada said.
"I have walked round by the bridge every day for a number of— for some years. It's very good for the character." Emrys bought two hot apples and handed her one without asking. "Mine is excellent."
"Modest, too."
"I've been told."
The towpath under Cutter's Row was wet cobbles and black weed, the canal at low water lapping below the edge. Down the bank spread a grey fan of the Row's sweepings: ash, eggshell, crockery, a boot.
Emrys stopped against the wall, three paces from the water. Exactly three. Ada suspected he had measured.
"You can come closer."
"I can see very well from here, thank you."
She didn't push. She crouched at the top of the fan and looked at it the way she'd look at a long dead circuit.
"What are you doing?" he asked, after a minute.
"Halving it." She drew a line across the ash with a stick. "Test the middle. Nothing there, throw away the top half and test the middle of what's left."
"That's—" Emrys paused. "That is annoyingly sensible."
"Fault-finding. Don't search the whole run. Split it."
On the third split she found bottle glass, cold and green. On the fourth, in the weed right at the water's lip, two curved pieces that caught the grey light and held it.
She closed her hand on them.
Warm.
Emrys was writing when she climbed back up. Without looking up he said, quietly, "I'll want to see how you do that again. For the record."
It sounded, very nearly, like respect.
Ninth bell rolled across the water, deep and slow. The lamps went up along Pell Street one by one, and rain began on the shop window.
Emrys arrived with his book and sat on the stool by the door, knees together, to witness, he said, whatever the Mender did tonight with glass of unknown ownership.
He had barely settled when the shop bell rang.
A girl stood on the step, about seven, with a scraped knee, a woolly hat, and a small lantern held in both hands like a bowl of soup.
"I'm Pim Hollis," she said. "I'm seven and three quarters. I fell off the wall by the bridge and my lantern chipped and Gran says you're to mend it and she'll pay you in eggs."
A chip on the shoulder of the glass, small and clean.
"What's it doing to you?"
"I keep losing my letters." Pim's face crumpled with effort. "A, B, C, all the way to M. And then it goes all foggy."
"Right," Ada said. "Stand there. Hands in your pockets. Don't touch the glass, whatever happens."
The readout bloomed over the little lantern. WICK. A thread of light traced the chip, and the bar waited, empty.
Ada laid her fingertip on the glass. It clicked, warm, like a stone in the sun.
The bar began to fill.
And the shop went away.

A kitchen, low and bright, seen from somewhere near the floor. A teacup with blue birds on it, in two pieces in small hands. A coal scuttle. The pieces going in under the coal, very carefully, and a tiny voice, Pim's voice, whispering, "It was the cat. It was the cat. We haven't got a cat."
The shop came back. The chip was gone. The bar was full and fading.
Pim took a breath. "N. O. P." She went pink with joy. "Q, R, S, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Zed!"
"Good," Ada said. Then, gently, "Is there anything you'd like to tell your gran, while you're feeling brave?"
Pim stared at her in horror.
"I didn't break the teacup," she said. Then she clapped both hands over her mouth, which was hard with a lantern in them.
Emrys made a small noise behind his book that might have been a cough.
"You could tell her," Ada said. "Before she finds out. That's all."
Pim fled into the rain. At the door she turned back and said, "Gran says you're not a real Mender because you haven't got a lantern," and then, kindly, "but I think you are," and was gone.
The shop bell settled.

Ada thought of Pim's scraped knee, and glanced at her own. Under her work trousers there was a scar, white, the size of a thumbprint, there since she was small. She'd told the story of it a hundred times, in pubs, in staff rooms, to every new apprentice.
She reached for the story now.
The scar was there. The story wasn't.
She tested it the way she'd tested the phone number. A wall? A bike? A step? Nothing came up. Not a fault. A gap where a wire used to be.
She took the brown paper from the drawer and wrote, under Mum's phone number:
2. My knee. How.
"What did it cost?" Emrys said.
She hadn't heard him get up. He was standing at the end of the bench, not quite looking at the list.
"Nothing much," Ada said.
"For the record—" He stopped. He looked at her for a moment, and then he closed his book without writing anything down.

He left an hour later, when it was plain she would not touch the shards while he sat there watching. They stayed with the Mender. He made her sign for them, in the margin, because there was no line for her.
Ada laid them out on the bench under the lamp. Sixteen pieces. Fourteen from the grate, two from the towpath.
The readout came up gold. WICK.
And under it, a word she hadn't seen before.
INCOMPLETE.
A line of light ran through the pieces, joining them edge to edge, all sixteen. Then it ran off the last one, out across the bare bench, and stopped, pointing at nothing.
An open circuit. A piece of the run that wasn't there.
The bar came up empty, with a notch cut out of its far end, as if it already knew it could never fill.
Ada sat back. Rule five: anything still open on the bench at first bell cracks worse. She was not going to start a job she couldn't close. Not on someone she couldn't even name.
So she opened the ledger instead.
Till now she'd left the crowded margins alone. Some part of her had not wanted to know any more.
She read them now.
Most were practical. Trim before you light. Never mend wet. Lost my best penknife today. Not to a mend. Just lost it. Some days are only days. She liked him for that.
Then, on the third page, boxed in heavy pencil:
You keep every face you mend. Even when the town doesn't.
She read it twice. She thought of Tobias, and of Pim, and wondered who would ever have to be remembered by her alone.
Further down, underlined so hard the nib had torn the paper:
Hot glass marks the hand that breaks it. Silver, and for life.
Ada looked at her own palms, plain and calloused. She thought of someone in Odile's front room, some night not long ago, holding a lantern while the glass went hot.
And at the bottom of the page, alone, small, as if he hadn't wanted to write it:
The last shard keeps the last hand.
She looked at the line of light on the bench, still pointing at the missing piece.
Somebody had swept this lantern up. Somebody had tipped it in the canal. And somebody, she thought, had kept one piece back.
One. Two. Three.

She turned to the back of the ledger, to the jobs: pages of names, streets and faults in the slanting hand. Then the slanting hand stopped partway down a page, as if he had simply put the pen down and walked away.
A long gap of blank ruled lines.
Then one more entry. Upright, round, pressed hard. Not his hand. Nothing like it.
Fane, I. Lantern brought in for cleaning. Collected by:
And then nothing. The line ran on, ruled and empty, to the edge of the page.
Ada sat very still while the rain ticked on the window and the town clock, across the water, did not.
Odile lived alone. Always had. The Register said one lantern, the shelf said empty, and nobody in that house had ever heard of anyone called Fane, I.
But someone had carried that lantern out of this shop, and had made very sure not to sign for it.
